title: The Second World War
tagline: Causes, course and results of the war that ended the old Europe and created the United Nations.

overview.intro: The Second World War was the largest conflict in human history, fought across Europe, Africa, Asia and the oceans, and it ended with the defeat of the three dictatorships, the atomic bomb and a completely new world order. This chapter begins with the causes — the unresolved grievances of Versailles, the failure of the League of Nations, the policy of appeasement and the agreements that encouraged aggression — then follows the course of the war from Poland to Hiroshima, and finally weighs the results: destruction on an unprecedented scale, the founding of the United Nations, the division of Europe into two armed camps and the beginning of decolonisation. The examination discipline is to keep causes under heads and to give dates for every campaign named.

Assess how far the Treaty of Versailles and the failure of the League of Nations were responsible for the war.

learn.title: The causes of the Second World War

blocks.text: The causes are best handled under five heads. The Treaty of Versailles: its war-guilt clause, reparations and territorial losses left Germany resentful, and every Nazi demand was framed as the correction of a national humiliation. The failure of the League of Nations: it had no army and its members would not act, so Japan left it in 1933 after Manchuria, Italy left in 1937 after Ethiopia, and the aggressions of the 1930s went unpunished, which taught the dictators that force paid. The rise of dictatorships: the militarist regimes in Germany, Italy and Japan needed constant success and therefore constant expansion, and rearmament in defiance of the treaty gave Germany the means. The policy of appeasement: Britain and France, haunted by the memory of 1914 to 1918 and short of arms, gave way at each stage — Hitler reoccupied the Rhineland in 1936, annexed Austria in March 1938 and was given the Sudetenland at the Munich Conference of September 1938, where the powers agreed to the dismemberment of Czechoslovakia in the belief that this was the last demand. The final stage was the Nazi-Soviet Pact of August 1939, which removed the fear of a two-front war for Germany and included a secret agreement to divide Poland, and when Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939 Britain and France declared war on 3 September 1939.

items: Versailles: war guilt, reparations and territorial losses supplied the grievance that Nazi propaganda used for twelve years.
The League of Nations failed to punish aggression in Manchuria and Ethiopia, and Japan and Italy left the League.
The dictatorships in Germany, Italy and Japan needed expansion to survive and rearmed in violation of treaties.
Appeasement: the Rhineland in 1936, Austria in March 1938 and the Sudetenland at Munich in September 1938 were all conceded.
The Nazi-Soviet Pact of August 1939 removed Germany’s fear of a two-front war and prepared the partition of Poland.
The invasion of Poland on 1 September 1939 and the British and French declarations of war on 3 September 1939 began the war.

Hitler reoccupied the demilitarised Rhineland with a handful of troops against the advice of his generals; had France acted then, Germany could have been stopped without a war.

items.meaning: The policy of conceding an aggressor’s demands in the hope of avoiding war, followed by Britain and France until 1939.
The September 1938 settlement handing the Sudetenland to Germany and abandoning Czechoslovakia.
The August 1939 agreement between Germany and the Soviet Union, with a secret clause to divide Poland.

blocks.text: Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939 with blitzkrieg tactics and, with the Soviet Union taking its share under the pact, Poland fell in weeks. The war then settled into the Phoney War until April 1940, when Germany overran Denmark and Norway and in May attacked the Low Countries and France, which fell in June 1940; the British Expeditionary Force escaped from Dunkirk in a remarkable flotilla of naval and civilian vessels. Britain under Churchill then stood alone: the Royal Air Force won the Battle of Britain in the summer and autumn of 1940, defeating the Luftwaffe’s attempt to win air superiority for an invasion, and the Blitz followed. In June 1941 Hitler launched Operation Barbarossa against the Soviet Union, reaching the gates of Moscow before the winter halted him; on 7 December 1941 Japan attacked the American fleet at Pearl Harbor, and Germany declared war on the United States, making the war truly global. The turning points came between 1942 and 1943: the Eighth Army broke the Axis in North Africa at El Alamein, the Allied landings in Sicily and Italy brought Mussolini down, and the German surrender at Stalingrad in February 1943 destroyed an entire army and the myth of invincibility. The Normandy landings of 6 June 1944 opened the second front, Paris was liberated in August 1944, and Germany collapsed in the spring of 1945, surrendering in May after Hitler’s suicide. Japan fought on until the atomic bombs were dropped on Hiroshima on 6 August and Nagasaki on 9 August 1945 and the Soviet Union declared war on Japan; the surrender was announced on 15 August 1945 and signed on 2 September 1945.

items: 1 September 1939: the invasion of Poland with blitzkrieg; Britain and France declare war on 3 September 1939.
1940: Denmark, Norway, the Low Countries and France fall; the British escape from Dunkirk; the Battle of Britain is won.
June 1941: Operation Barbarossa opens the eastern front; the German advance stalls before Moscow.
7 December 1941: Pearl Harbor brings the United States into the war, and the war becomes global.
1942 to 1943: El Alamein, the fall of Mussolini and the surrender at Stalingrad turn the tide.
6 June 1944: the Normandy landings open the second front; Germany surrenders in May 1945.
August 1945: the atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki and the Soviet declaration of war on Japan end the war on 2 September 1945.

The encirclement and surrender of the German Sixth Army was the psychological turning point of the war in Europe.

learn.title: The results of the Second World War

blocks.text: The results fall under four heads. Human and material: about fifty million people died, a large proportion of them civilians, whole cities lay in ruins, and the material destruction was greater than in any earlier war. Political: four great European powers — Britain, France, Germany and Italy — were exhausted or defeated, and two non-European superpowers, the United States and the Soviet Union, faced each other across a divided Europe, with Germany itself divided into occupation zones and later into two states. Legal and moral: the Nuremberg and Tokyo trials charged the Nazi and Japanese leaders with crimes against peace, war crimes and crimes against humanity, and the doctrine that obedience to orders is no defence for atrocities entered international law. Institutional and colonial: the United Nations was founded in 1945 to replace the failed League and to prevent a third war, the colonial powers were weakened and discredited, and within two decades most of Asia and Africa had become independent, while the atom bomb introduced the possibility of the destruction of civilisation itself, which framed the Cold War rivalry that followed.

items: About fifty million dead, a great proportion of them civilians, and cities and industries destroyed across Europe and Asia.
The end of the old European great powers and the rise of two superpowers, the United States and the Soviet Union.
Germany divided and Europe partitioned into armed blocs, which became the Cold War.
The Nuremberg and Tokyo trials established that war criminals answer individually, and that obeying orders is no defence.
The United Nations was founded in 1945 to maintain peace and security in place of the failed League.
The weakening of the colonial powers accelerated the independence of Asia and Africa, and the atomic bomb opened the nuclear age.

India, Indonesia, Vietnam, Ghana and dozens of others became independent between 1945 and 1963, because the war had exhausted the imperial powers and discredited colonial rule.

A state with global military and economic reach; the United States and the Soviet Union after 1945.
The state of hostility without direct war between the United States-led and Soviet-led blocs after 1945.
The era beginning in 1945 in which nuclear weapons made the destruction of civilisation possible.

learn.title: How far were Versailles and the League responsible for the war?

blocks.text: This judgement question is best answered by weighing each factor and then combining them. Versailles was responsible in the sense that it supplied the grievance, the language and a good part of the audience for Nazism: the war-guilt clause and reparations embittered the educated middle class, the territorial losses gave specific demands to make, and the stipulation that Germany alone was guilty made the republic that signed it look treacherous. But Versailles alone did not produce the war: many of its victims accepted the settlement, and it was the depression after 1929 that turned millions of voters to Hitler rather than the treaty itself. The League of Nations was responsible in a different way: by failing to act over Manchuria in 1931 and Ethiopia in 1935 it demonstrated that aggression would go unpunished, and its failure was compounded by the absence of the United States, the refusal of members to keep disarmament promises and the British and French preference for appeasement. The most defensible judgement is therefore that Versailles created the grievance, the League’s failures created the opportunity, appeasement created the confidence, and the dictatorships themselves — with their need for expansion and their rearmament — created the war. Each was necessary; none alone was sufficient.

items: Versailles supplied the grievance and the propaganda, and discredited the German republic that accepted it.
The depression, not the treaty alone, delivered the mass vote to the Nazis in 1930 to 1932.
The League failed over Manchuria and Ethiopia, and lacked the members, the army and the will to act.
Appeasement, especially Munich in 1938, taught Hitler that concessions would continue.
Judgement: grievance, opportunity, confidence and the dictatorships’ own expansionism together produced the war.

items.note: Versailles wrote the grievance, the League supplied the opportunity and appeasement supplied the confidence, but only the decision of the dictators to use force made war certain.
The League had no army, no United States support and members unwilling to keep disarmament promises, so its failure was structural rather than a matter of bad luck in two crises.

questions.prompt: State four causes of the Second World War.
questions.answer: The Treaty of Versailles left Germany bitter through its war-guilt clause, reparations and territorial losses, which Nazi propaganda used. The League of Nations failed to punish aggression in Manchuria and Ethiopia, and Japan and Italy left the League. The rise of the dictatorships brought rearmament in violation of the treaties and a need for constant expansion. The policy of appeasement, culminating in the Munich Agreement of September 1938, taught Hitler that the democratic powers would give way, and the Nazi-Soviet Pact of August 1939 removed his fear of a two-front war.

questions.prompt: What were the main results of the Second World War?
questions.answer: About fifty million people died, a large proportion of them civilians, and cities and industry lay ruined across Europe and Asia. The old European powers were exhausted and two superpowers, the United States and the Soviet Union, faced each other across a divided Europe, with Germany itself partitioned. The Nuremberg and Tokyo trials established that individuals answer for war crimes and crimes against humanity. The United Nations was founded in 1945 to keep the peace, the atomic bomb opened the nuclear age, and the weakness of the colonial powers accelerated the independence of Asia and Africa.

questions.prompt: Mention two turning points of the Second World War.
questions.answer: The Battle of Britain in the summer and autumn of 1940 defeated the Luftwaffe and prevented the invasion of the British Isles. The German surrender at Stalingrad in February 1943 destroyed an entire army and the myth of German invincibility, and the Normandy landings of 6 June 1944 opened the second front in the west.
questions.explanation: Any two of the Battle of Britain, Stalingrad, El Alamein, the Normandy landings and Pearl Harbor as the global turning point.

questions.prompt: Describe the course of the Second World War from the invasion of Poland to the surrender of Japan.
questions.answer: Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939 using blitzkrieg tactics, and Britain and France declared war on 3 September 1939. After the Phoney War, Germany overran Denmark and Norway in April 1940 and in May attacked the Low Countries and France, which fell in June 1940, though the British Expeditionary Force was evacuated from Dunkirk. Britain then stood alone, and the Royal Air Force won the Battle of Britain in 1940, defeating the attempt to win air superiority for an invasion. In June 1941 Germany launched Operation Barbarossa against the Soviet Union and reached the outskirts of Moscow before the winter stopped the advance. On 7 December 1941 Japan attacked Pearl Harbor and Germany declared war on the United States, making the war global. The tide turned between 1942 and 1943: the Eighth Army won at El Alamein, the Allies took North Africa and Sicily and brought down Mussolini, and the German surrender at Stalingrad in February 1943 destroyed an army. The Normandy landings of 6 June 1944 opened the second front, Paris was liberated in August 1944, and Germany surrendered in May 1945 after Hitler’s suicide. Japan refused to surrender until atomic bombs were dropped on Hiroshima on 6 August and Nagasaki on 9 August 1945 and the Soviet Union declared war; the surrender was signed on 2 September 1945.
questions.explanation: A chronological narrative with the key dates: Poland, France, Britain, Barbarossa, Pearl Harbor, Stalingrad, Normandy, May 1945 and August to September 1945.

questions.prompt: How far was the Treaty of Versailles responsible for the Second World War?
questions.answer: The case that Versailles was responsible rests on three arguments. Its war-guilt clause, Article 231, declared Germany alone guilty, which was resented even by Germans who had accepted defeat and made the Weimar government that signed it look like an instrument of foreign dictation. The reparations and the economic disruption that followed, including the French occupation of the Ruhr in 1923 and the hyperinflation of that year, destroyed the savings and the confidence of the middle class, so that the republic never won the loyalty of the population. The territorial losses — Alsace-Lorraine, the Polish Corridor, the colonies — and the military limits supplied Hitler with ready-made grievances which he converted into a programme of rearmament and revision presented as national regeneration. The case against an exclusive blame is equally strong: the treaty’s terms were in many respects milder than earlier peace settlements, the depression of 1929 rather than the treaty delivered the mass Nazi vote, and Hitler’s decisions — rearmament, the invasion of Poland, the war against the Soviet Union — went far beyond any revision of Versailles. My judgement is that the treaty supplied the grievance and the propaganda on which Nazism fed, but the war itself was produced by the choices of the dictators in a crisis the depression created.
questions.explanation: Three arguments for, three against, then a verdict distinguishing grievance from decision.

questions.prompt: Explain the policy of appeasement and show how it encouraged the aggressors.
questions.answer: Appeasement was the policy, followed especially by Britain and France between 1933 and 1939, of conceding an aggressor’s demands in the hope of avoiding a general war. It was driven by the memory of the slaughter of 1914 to 1918, by economic depression and by slow rearmament, and it was encouraged by the belief that the Versailles settlement had been unjust to Germany. Its course was a sequence of concessions: the Anglo-German Naval Agreement of 1935 allowed Germany to rebuild its navy, the remilitarisation of the Rhineland in 1936 was met with no action, the annexation of Austria in March 1938 was accepted, and at Munich in September 1938 Britain and France agreed to the surrender of the Sudetenland without consulting Czechoslovakia, which was dismembered within six months. The effect on the aggressors was to teach them that the democracies would not fight: each success convinced Hitler that the next demand would also be granted, and it convinced Japan and Italy that the League and collective security could be defied with impunity. Appeasement ended only with the guarantee to Poland in March 1939, but by then Germany was rearmed, Austria and the Sudetenland were absorbed and the strategic position of the Western powers had deteriorated beyond recovery.
questions.explanation: Definition, causes of the policy, the sequence of concessions, and the lesson each aggressor drew from it.
